nodes.title: Historical Evolution of Indian Constitution (1773-1947)
prelimsNote: Regulating Act 1773: Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings); Supreme Court set up at Calcutta (1774).
Pitt's India Act 1784: Board of Control → 'dual government'; Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except tea and trade with China.
Charter Act 1833: Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (Bentinck) — final step of centralisation; Charter Act 1853 introduced open competition for civil services.
Morley–Minto 1909: separate electorate for Muslims; GoI Act 1919: dyarchy in provinces (reserved vs transferred subjects — justice, police, land revenue were RESERVED).
GoI Act 1935: provincial autonomy, dyarchy at the Centre (never operated), Federal Court (1937); residuary powers vested in the Governor-General — a favourite UPSC trap.

nodes.title: Constituent Assembly & Constitutional Making Process
prelimsNote: Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946); members indirectly elected by provincial assemblies (single transferable vote) — not by universal adult franchise.
First meeting 9 Dec 1946 (Sachchidananda Sinha, temporary President); Rajendra Prasad elected President on 11 Dec 1946.
Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, adopted 22 Jan 1947; Drafting Committee under B.R. Ambedkar set up 29 Aug 1947.
Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949 (now Constitution Day, declared 2015); came into force 26 Jan 1950 — but citizenship, elections and provisional Parliament provisions took effect on 26 Nov 1949.
Trap: the Drafting Committee was NOT set up on 26 Nov 1949, and the CA also functioned as the first Parliament (provisional).

nodes.title: Salient Features of Indian Constitution
prelimsNote: Bulk of the structure borrowed from the GoI Act 1935 (federal scheme, office of Governor, emergency, PSCs).

Borrowings: parliamentary system & rule of law (UK), FRs & judicial review (USA), DPSP (Ireland), residuary powers with Centre (Canada), Concurrent List (Australia), suspension of FRs in emergency (Weimar Germany), procedure established by law (Japan).
Unique blend: rigidity + flexibility, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, universal adult franchise, independent bodies (ECI, CAG, UPSC).
'Constitutional government' = limited government; the chief purpose of a constitution is to define and limit the powers of government (UPSC 2020, 2021, 2023).

nodes.title: Federal vs Unitary Features of Indian Constitution
prelimsNote: Federal features: dual polity, written & supreme Constitution, division of powers, independent judiciary, bicameralism.

Unitary features: strong Centre, single Constitution & citizenship, integrated judiciary, All-India Services, Governor appointed by Centre, emergency provisions, Art 3 (States can be reorganised without consent).
Art 1: 'Union of States' — Indian federation is NOT the result of an agreement among states and states cannot secede (UPSC 2017 trap).
Federalism is part of the basic structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994); India often described as 'quasi-federal' (K.C. Wheare).

nodes.title: Parliamentary vs Presidential System — Comparison
prelimsNote: Parliamentary system = executive responsible to, and removable by, the legislature (UPSC 2020) — collective responsibility to Lok Sabha (Art 75(3)).
Nominal (President) vs real (PM & Council of Ministers) executive; dissolution of Lok Sabha; ministers must be MPs (or become one within 6 months).
Indian vs British model: India has a written Constitution with judicial review, so Parliament is NOT sovereign; head of State is elected (republic).
Presidential (USA): fixed tenure, strict separation of powers, executive not removable by legislature except by impeachment.

nodes.title: Preamble — Values & Constitutional Philosophy
prelimsNote: Based on the Objectives Resolution (Nehru, 13 Dec 1946; adopted 22 Jan 1947); enacted last, after the rest of the Constitution.
Amended only once — 42nd Amendment 1976 added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'.
Part of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati 1973, overruling Berubari 1960; reaffirmed LIC 1995) — but neither a source of power nor a limit on legislature; non-justiciable.
Trap: 'economic liberty' is NOT in the Preamble — it guarantees liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship (UPSC 2017).
Order of words: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; justice — social, economic and political (inspired by the Russian Revolution).

nodes.title: Fundamental Rights — Scope, Limitations & Judicial Interpretation
prelimsNote: Part III (Arts 12–35); Art 13 is the basis of judicial review; Arts 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 are available only to citizens, the rest to all persons.
Arts 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during a national emergency (44th Amendment 1978); Art 19 is suspended automatically only when emergency is on grounds of war/external aggression.
Art 32 writs: mandamus does not lie against a private body unless it performs a public duty; any person can seek quo warranto (UPSC 2022).
Art 21 expanded: Maneka Gandhi 1978 (fair procedure), right to privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), right to choose a spouse (Hadiya 2018); Art 21A added by 86th Amendment 2002.
Right to property removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment → now a legal right under Art 300A; Art 18: national awards are not 'titles' (Balaji Raghavan 1996).

nodes.title: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) — Implementation & Conflicts with FR
prelimsNote: Part IV (Arts 36–51), borrowed from the Irish Constitution; non-justiciable (Art 37) but 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.
The ideal of the welfare state is declared in the DPSP (UPSC 2015, 2020) — not in the FRs.
Added later: Arts 39A, 43A, 48A and 39(f) by the 42nd Amendment; Art 38(2) by the 44th; Art 45 recast by the 86th; Art 43B (co-operatives) by the 97th.
Key articles: Art 40 village panchayats, Art 44 Uniform Civil Code, Art 48 organisation of agriculture & cattle, Art 50 separation of judiciary from executive.
Minerva Mills 1980: harmony and balance between FR and DPSP is part of the basic structure; DPSP are NOT limitations on the legislature (UPSC 2017 trap).

nodes.title: Fundamental Duties
prelimsNote: Part IVA, Art 51A — added by the 42nd Amendment 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; inspired by the USSR Constitution.
Originally 10 duties; the 11th (parents/guardians to provide education to children 6–14) added by the 86th Amendment 2002.
Non-justiciable — no writ lies to enforce them, but Parliament can enforce them by law; apply only to citizens.
Include: respect the Constitution, flag & anthem; protect environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property — but NOT 'pay taxes' or 'vote'.

nodes.title: Basic Structure Doctrine — Evolution & Significance
prelimsNote: Not defined anywhere in the Constitution — a judicial creation (UPSC 2020).
Kesavananda Bharati 1973 (13 judges, 7:6): Parliament can amend any part but not the basic structure; overruled Golaknath 1967.
Minerva Mills 1980 struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Art 368 added by the 42nd Amendment; Waman Rao 1981 and I.R. Coelho 2007: Ninth Schedule laws after 24 Apr 1973 are open to review.
Elements recognised: supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, federalism, secularism, free & fair elections (Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain 1975), independence of judiciary (NJAC case 2015).

nodes.title: Constitutional Amendments — Process, Key Amendments & Pending Amendments
prelimsNote: Art 368 (Part XX) — three routes: simple majority (outside Art 368, e.g. Arts 2–4, Fifth/Sixth Schedules), special majority, and special majority + ratification by half the states.
Ratification needed for federal provisions: election of President, SC/HCs, Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, Art 368 itself.
Amendment bill: introduced in either House, by a minister or private member, needs NO prior Presidential recommendation; NO joint sitting; President must give assent (24th Amendment).
Landmarks: 1st (1951, Ninth Schedule), 42nd (1976, 'mini-Constitution'), 44th (1978), 73rd/74th (1992), 86th (2002, Art 21A), 101st (2016, GST), 103rd (2019, EWS), 106th (2023, women's reservation).

nodes.title: India as a Welfare State
prelimsNote: The ideal of a welfare state is declared by the Directive Principles (Art 38) — UPSC asked this in 2015 and 2020.
The Preamble's 'justice — social, economic and political' and 'Socialist' (42nd Amendment) support the welfare-state goal.
DPSPs such as Arts 39, 41, 42, 43, 47 set welfare obligations; they are non-justiciable.
Trap: welfare state is NOT located in the Fundamental Rights or the Seventh Schedule.

nodes.title: Centre-State Legislative Relations — Union, State & Concurrent Lists
prelimsNote: Part XI (Arts 245–255) and the Seventh Schedule — Union, State and Concurrent Lists; residuary powers with Parliament (Art 248, Canadian model).

Parliament may legislate on State List: Art 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 present & voting, valid 1 year), Art 250 (emergency), Art 252 (two or more states consent), Art 253 (international agreements — UPSC 2013).
Art 254: in conflict on a Concurrent List subject, Union law prevails unless the State law reserved for and received the President's assent.
42nd Amendment moved five subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, weights & measures, protection of wild animals & birds, administration of justice.

nodes.title: Centre-State Administrative Relations
prelimsNote: Arts 256–263: States must comply with Union laws; Union can give directions (Art 256, 257); Art 365 — failure to comply can lead to Art 356.
Art 355: duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance (UPSC 2023).
Art 262: Parliament may exclude SC jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes (Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956).
All-India Services under Art 312 — new service created on a Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 majority.

nodes.title: Centre-State Financial Relations & Fiscal Federalism
prelimsNote: Arts 264–293: divisible pool shared under Art 270; grants-in-aid under Art 275 (statutory) and Art 282 (discretionary).
Art 293: a State owing money to the Centre needs the Centre's consent to borrow (UPSC 2018).
GST: Art 246A (concurrent taxing power), Art 269A (IGST on inter-state supply), Art 279A (GST Council) — 101st Amendment 2016.
Before GST, sales tax was imposed and collected by the State (UPSC 2014).

nodes.title: Governor — Role, Discretionary Powers & Politicisation
prelimsNote: Appointed by the President (Art 155), holds office during the President's pleasure (Art 156) — removal must not be arbitrary (B.P. Singhal 2010).
Same person can be Governor of two or more states (7th Amendment 1956); qualifications: citizen, 35 years.
Art 361: no criminal proceedings during term, not answerable to courts for exercise of powers (UPSC 2018).
Discretion: reserving bills for the President (Art 200), report under Art 356, choosing a CM in a hung house; Nabam Rebia 2016 limited discretion over the Assembly.
Sarkaria Commission: Governor should be an eminent person from outside the state, not active in local politics (UPSC 2019).

nodes.title: Misuse of Article 356 — President's Rule
prelimsNote: Art 356: Proclamation must be approved by both Houses within 2 months by simple majority; 6 months at a time, maximum 3 years.
Beyond one year only if a national emergency is in force AND the ECI certifies elections cannot be held (44th Amendment).
S.R. Bommai 1994: majority to be tested on the floor; proclamation is judicially reviewable; Assembly can be suspended but not dissolved before Parliament's approval.
During President's Rule Parliament legislates for the State (may delegate to the President); these laws continue after it ends until changed — the High Court is NOT affected (UPSC 2017, 2018).

nodes.title: Inter-State Council & Dispute Resolution Mechanisms
prelimsNote: Inter-State Council (Art 263) set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation; chaired by the Prime Minister.
Inter-state water disputes: Art 262 + Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956 (tribunals).
Zonal Councils are statutory (States Reorganisation Act 1956), not constitutional; chaired by the Union Home Minister.
Arts 301–307: freedom of trade and commerce throughout India; Art 261: full faith and credit to public acts and judicial proceedings.

nodes.title: Special Category Status & Special Packages for States
prelimsNote: Special Category Status is NOT mentioned in the Constitution — introduced in 1969 on the NDC's approval (Gadgil formula, 5th Finance Commission).
Criteria: hilly terrain, low population density or large tribal share, strategic border location, economic backwardness, non-viable finances.
The 14th Finance Commission recommended doing away with the distinction; SCS states still get favourable Centre–State sharing in CSS (90:10).
Trap: SCS differs from 'special provisions' for states under Arts 371–371J, which are constitutional.

nodes.title: Centrally Sponsored Schemes — Issues & Rationalisation
prelimsNote: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are implemented by States with a Centre–State cost-sharing pattern (typically 60:40; 90:10 for NE and Himalayan states).
Constitutional basis for discretionary grants: Art 282.
2015 Sub-Group of CMs (NITI Aayog) rationalised CSS into 'core of the core', 'core' and 'optional' schemes.
Central Sector schemes are 100% Centre-funded and implemented by central agencies — differ from CSS.

nodes.title: GST & Cooperative Federalism
prelimsNote: 101st Amendment 2016; GST in force from 1 July 2017; GST Council under Art 279A chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
Voting: Centre has 1/3 weight, States 2/3; decisions need 3/4 of weighted votes present.
Mohit Minerals 2022: Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding on Parliament and State legislatures.
Alcohol for human consumption is outside GST; petroleum products are within GST but levied only from a date the Council recommends.

nodes.title: Finance Commission — Role, Devolution & Analysis
prelimsNote: Art 280: constituted by the President every 5 years; chairman + 4 members; qualifications set by the Finance Commission (Misc. Provisions) Act 1951.
Recommends vertical (Centre–States) and horizontal (among States) sharing of taxes and grants-in-aid; recommendations are advisory.
15th FC (N.K. Singh): 41% devolution; criteria — income distance, population (2011), area, forest & ecology, demographic performance, tax & fiscal efforts (UPSC 2023).
14th FC raised devolution to 42% and recommended doing away with the special category distinction (UPSC 2015).

nodes.title: Demand for Smaller States & State Formation Issues
prelimsNote: Art 3: Parliament can form new States/alter boundaries by simple majority; bill needs the President's recommendation; the affected State's views are NOT binding.
Art 4: such laws are not amendments under Art 368.
States Reorganisation Act 1956 (Fazl Ali Commission) — linguistic reorganisation; Andhra State 1953 the first linguistic state.
Cession of territory to a foreign country needs a constitutional amendment (Berubari 1960 → 9th Amendment; 100th Amendment 2015 for the India–Bangladesh land boundary).

nodes.title: Parliament — Structure, Functions & Composition (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha)
prelimsNote: Art 79: Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha; Rajya Sabha max 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated); Anglo-Indian nomination to Lok Sabha ended by the 104th Amendment (2020).
Rajya Sabha is permanent — one-third retire every second year; gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months (Art 85); quorum is one-tenth of members.
Exclusive Lok Sabha powers: money bills originate there and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to it; no-confidence motion only in Lok Sabha.
Rajya Sabha special powers: Art 249 (State List) and Art 312 (new All-India Service); approving an Emergency needs BOTH Houses — not an exclusive Lok Sabha power (UPSC 2022).
Deputy Speaker is elected on a date fixed by the Speaker; there is NO mandatory rule that the post goes to the opposition (UPSC 2022).

nodes.title: State Legislatures — Legislative Assembly & Legislative Council
prelimsNote: Legislative Council created/abolished by Parliament on a State Assembly resolution by special majority (Art 169); exists in 6 states.
Size: not more than 1/3 of the Assembly, not less than 40 (Art 171); 1/3 elected by MLAs, 1/3 by local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated by Governor.
Council can delay an ordinary bill up to 4 months and a money bill only 14 days — no joint sitting at state level.
Speaker does NOT vacate office on dissolution of the Assembly — continues until the new Assembly first meets (UPSC 2018).

nodes.title: Law Making Process in India
prelimsNote: Money bill (Art 110): only in Lok Sabha, on President's recommendation; Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days; Speaker's certificate is final.
Finance Bill under Art 117(1): introduced only in Lok Sabha, but Rajya Sabha CAN amend or reject it; a joint sitting is possible — not 'necessary' (UPSC 2023).
Lapse: bills pending in Lok Sabha lapse on its dissolution; a bill pending in Rajya Sabha not yet passed by Lok Sabha does NOT lapse; prorogation does not lapse bills (UPSC 2016).
Joint sitting (Art 108) is presided by the Speaker; not available for money bills or constitutional amendment bills.
President has no veto over a money bill (cannot return it) and must assent to a constitutional amendment bill; no time limit is prescribed for assent to ordinary bills (UPSC 2023).

nodes.title: Parliamentary Committees — Role & Functions
prelimsNote: Estimates Committee (30 members, all Lok Sabha) is the largest committee and has NO Rajya Sabha members (UPSC 2014, 2018).
Public Accounts Committee: 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS); chairman from the opposition by convention since 1967; examines CAG audit reports.
Committee on Public Undertakings: 22 members (15 + 7); Departmentally Related Standing Committees (since 1993) — 24 committees.
Committee on Subordinate Legislation scrutinises delegated legislation (UPSC 2018); ministers cannot be members of financial committees.

nodes.title: Parliamentary Privileges & Immunity
prelimsNote: Arts 105 (Parliament) and 194 (State legislatures); not codified by law — determined by convention and precedent.
Immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the House; freedom from arrest only in civil cases (40 days before/after a session).
Privileges also extend to persons entitled to speak in a House — Attorney General and ministers (Art 105(4)).
Sita Soren 2024 (7 judges): bribery to vote/speak is NOT protected by privilege — overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao 1998.

nodes.title: Anti-Defection Law — Tenth Schedule & Issues
prelimsNote: Tenth Schedule added by the 52nd Amendment 1985; the 91st Amendment 2003 deleted the 'split' (one-third) exception — only merger by 2/3 of legislators is exempt.
A nominated member may join a party within 6 months of taking the seat; an independent member who joins any party is disqualified (UPSC 2022).
Presiding officer decides; decision is subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan 1992).
The law prescribes NO time limit for deciding (UPSC 2022); the SC (Keisham Meghachandra 2020) said decisions should ordinarily come within three months.

nodes.title: Ordinance Making Power — Misuse & Reforms
prelimsNote: Art 123 (President) / Art 213 (Governor): only when the legislature (either House) is not in session; same force as an Act.
Must be laid before Parliament and expires 6 weeks after reassembly — maximum life about 6 months + 6 weeks; cannot amend the Constitution.

D.C. Wadhwa 1987 and Krishna Kumar Singh 2017: re-promulgation without placing before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution; satisfaction is justiciable (38th Amendment's bar removed by 44th).
Ordinance can be withdrawn any time by the President on the Council of Ministers' advice.

nodes.title: Women's Reservation in Parliament
prelimsNote: 106th Amendment 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam): one-third seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly (Arts 330A, 332A, 239AA).
Includes one-third of seats reserved for SC/ST; does NOT cover Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils.
Takes effect after delimitation based on the first census after commencement; lasts 15 years; seats rotate after each delimitation.
Women already have one-third reservation in Panchayats (Art 243D) and Municipalities (Art 243T).

nodes.title: Simultaneous Elections — Feasibility & Debate
prelimsNote: Simultaneous elections were held in 1951–52, 1957, 1962 and 1967; the cycle broke from 1968–69.
Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) supported simultaneous polls; the Ram Nath Kovind High-Level Committee reported in 2024.
Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill 2024 proposed aligning Lok Sabha and Assembly terms (new Art 82A); referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (status as of late 2024).
Constitutional articles involved: 83 and 172 (duration of Houses), 85 and 174 (dissolution), 356.

nodes.title: Declining Standards of Parliamentary Functioning
prelimsNote: Question Hour: first hour of a sitting; starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries, unstarred get written answers.
Zero Hour is an Indian innovation (since 1962) not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.
Adjournment motion is moved only in Lok Sabha, needs 50 members' support and involves an element of censure.
Parliamentary control over the executive works through motions, Question Hour and supplementary questions (UPSC 2017).

nodes.title: Delegated Legislation & Issues
prelimsNote: Delegated legislation: Parliament lays down policy; the executive frames rules — essential legislative functions cannot be delegated (In re Delhi Laws Act 1951).
Scrutiny by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation in each House (UPSC 2018).
Rules are laid before Parliament and can be modified or annulled.
Excessive delegation can be struck down by courts.

nodes.title: President of India — Powers, Functions & Role
prelimsNote: Electoral college: elected MPs + elected MLAs of States, Delhi and Puducherry (70th Amendment 1992) — nominated members and MLCs do NOT vote (UPSC 2023).
Value of an MLA's vote = State population (1971 census) ÷ (elected MLAs × 1000); value of an MP's vote is uniform across both Houses (UPSC 2018, 2023).
Election disputes decided by the Supreme Court; acts done before an election is declared void remain valid (Art 71); election cannot be postponed because some Assemblies are dissolved.
Impeachment (Art 61): only for violation of the Constitution, 2/3 of total membership of each House; nominated members take part.
Art 72 pardoning powers; Art 123 ordinances; Art 143 advisory reference to the SC; no time limit prescribed for assent to ordinary bills.

nodes.title: Prime Minister & Council of Ministers
prelimsNote: Art 74: aid and advice binding on the President (42nd and 44th Amendments); Art 75(3): collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.
Council of Ministers capped at 15% of Lok Sabha strength including the PM (91st Amendment 2003) — not 15% of total Parliament.
Ranks (Cabinet, MoS with independent charge, MoS, Deputy) are NOT classified in the Constitution (UPSC 2022); 'Cabinet' is mentioned only in Art 352.
A non-member can be a minister for 6 months; Art 77(3): Government of India (Allocation/Transaction of Business) Rules (UPSC 2014).

nodes.title: Governor — Constitutional Role vs Political Reality
prelimsNote: Art 163: the Governor acts on the Council of Ministers' aid and advice except where required to act in his discretion.
Art 200 options on a bill: assent, withhold, return (except money bills) or reserve for the President (Art 201).
State of Punjab v Governor (2023): a Governor cannot sit on bills indefinitely and must return them to the Assembly if withholding assent.
The Governor's address to the Assembly is prepared by the State government and reflects its policy.
Trap: the Governor as university Chancellor is a statutory role, not a constitutional one.

nodes.title: Emergency Provisions — National, State & Financial Emergency
prelimsNote: National Emergency (Art 352): war, external aggression or armed rebellion ('internal disturbance' replaced by 44th Amendment); approval by both Houses within 1 month by special majority; renewal every 6 months.
Revocation: Lok Sabha resolution by simple majority (special sitting on notice by 1/10 of members); the President must revoke if Lok Sabha disapproves.
Art 358: Art 19 suspended automatically only for war/external aggression; Art 359: enforcement of other FRs may be suspended — except Arts 20 and 21.
Financial Emergency (Art 360) has never been proclaimed; national emergencies were proclaimed in 1962, 1971 and 1975.

nodes.title: Coalition Government — Challenges & Stability
prelimsNote: Collective responsibility (Art 75(3)) binds all ministers of a coalition: they swim and sink together.
Sarkaria Commission order for inviting a party in a hung house: pre-poll alliance, single largest party with others' support, post-poll coalition, etc.
Anti-defection law limits switching but permits a 2/3 merger.
Rameshwar Prasad 2006: dissolution of an Assembly to prevent government formation was unconstitutional.

nodes.title: Supreme Court — Guardian of Constitution & Fundamental Rights
prelimsNote: Art 124: strength fixed by Parliament (not the President) — currently 34 judges including the CJI (UPSC 2014).
Original jurisdiction (Art 131) over Centre–State and inter-state disputes; advisory jurisdiction (Art 143) — advice not binding (UPSC 2011).
Art 129: court of record with power to punish for contempt; Art 137: review; Art 142: complete justice — orders can override ordinary law (UPSC 2019).
Art 128: retired judges can be requested to sit with the President's consent (UPSC 2021); Art 127: ad hoc judges.
Removal (Art 124(4)): motion signed by 100 LS or 50 RS members; Speaker/Chairman can admit or reject it; procedure under the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968.

nodes.title: Judicial Review — Scope & Limits
prelimsNote: Judicial review rests on Arts 13, 32, 136, 226 and 227 — the phrase itself is not used in the Constitution.
It is part of the basic structure (Kesavananda 1973; L. Chandra Kumar 1997 for High Courts' power over tribunal decisions).
Ninth Schedule laws placed after 24 Apr 1973 are open to review (I.R. Coelho 2007).
Indian Constitution follows 'procedure established by law' (Art 21) — courts have read in fairness and reasonableness (Maneka Gandhi 1978).

nodes.title: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) — Evolution & Misuse
prelimsNote: Originated in the late 1970s–80s (Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer); locus standi relaxed in S.P. Gupta 1981.
Filed under Art 32 (SC) or Art 226 (HC); even letters can be treated as petitions (epistolary jurisdiction).
Hussainara Khatoon 1979 (undertrials) is one of the earliest PILs.
PIL is a judicial innovation — not mentioned in the Constitution or any statute.

nodes.title: Judicial Activism vs Judicial Overreach
prelimsNote: Activism: Vishaka 1997 guidelines filled a legislative vacuum until the 2013 Act; Art 142 used for 'complete justice'.
Overreach concern: courts entering policy domains reserved for the legislature/executive.
Separation of powers is part of the basic structure, though India has no rigid separation (Ram Jawaya Kapur 1955).
Art 141: SC law is binding on all courts; Art 144: all authorities must act in aid of the SC.

nodes.title: Collegium System & Judicial Appointments (NJAC Controversy)
prelimsNote: First Judges case (S.P. Gupta 1981): executive primacy; Second Judges case (1993): collegium created; Third Judges case (1998): CJI + 4 senior-most judges for SC appointments.
99th Amendment 2014 (NJAC) struck down in 2015 (Fourth Judges case) for violating judicial independence — a basic feature.
Art 124(2): appointment by the President after consultation; Art 217 (HC judges); Art 222 (transfer of HC judges).
Memorandum of Procedure governs the actual appointment process.

nodes.title: Judicial Accountability & Transparency
prelimsNote: Removal under Arts 124(4)/217 via the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968; no SC or HC judge has been removed so far (V. Ramaswami motion failed in 1993).
Office of the CJI is a 'public authority' under RTI (Subhash Chandra Agarwal 2019).
In-house procedure (1999) and Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997) are internal mechanisms.
Contempt of Courts Act 1971 was enacted following the H.N. Sanyal Committee report (UPSC 2022).

nodes.title: High Courts & Subordinate Courts — Structure & Issues
prelimsNote: Common High Court for two or more states/UTs allowed (Art 231) — e.g. Bombay, Guwahati, Punjab & Haryana (UPSC 2012).
HC judges retire at 62 (SC at 65); Art 226 writ jurisdiction is wider than Art 32 ('for any other purpose').
Art 227 superintendence over subordinate courts; Art 215 HC is a court of record with contempt power.
District judges appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court (Art 233); HCs can exercise judicial review (UPSC 2019).

nodes.title: Fast Track Courts, Gram Nyayalayas & Access to Justice
prelimsNote: Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008: courts at the intermediate panchayat level, presided by a Nyayadhikari (Judicial Magistrate First Class), can work as mobile courts (UPSC 2016).
Handle specified civil and criminal cases; follow summary procedure and need not be bound by the Evidence Act strictly.
Fast Track Courts began in 2000 on the 11th Finance Commission's recommendation; Fast Track Special Courts (2019) for rape and POCSO cases.
Art 39A (free legal aid, 42nd Amendment) underpins access-to-justice measures.

nodes.title: Lok Adalat, NALSA & Alternative Dispute Resolution
prelimsNote: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 gave statutory status to Lok Adalats; NALSA constituted in 1995 — CJI is Patron-in-Chief.
Lok Adalat award = civil court decree, final and binding, no appeal, no court fee.
Free legal services: SC/ST, women, children, persons with disability, industrial workmen, persons in custody, those below the notified income limit (UPSC 2020).
Permanent Lok Adalats (2002 amendment) handle disputes over public utility services.

nodes.title: All India Judicial Services — Debate & Feasibility
prelimsNote: Art 312 (added by the 42nd Amendment) provides for an All-India Judicial Service.
Created by Parliament after a Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 present and voting.
It cannot include posts inferior to a district judge (Art 312(3)).
No AIJS has been created so far.

nodes.title: National Litigation Policy & Pendency Crisis
prelimsNote: National Litigation Policy (2010) aimed to make government an efficient, responsible litigant.
National Judicial Data Grid (eCourts) tracks pendency in real time.
Art 224A allows retired judges to sit as ad hoc judges in High Courts (Lok Prahari 2021 guidelines).
Art 39A and Lok Adalats/ADR are the constitutional-statutory tools against pendency.

nodes.title: Election Commission of India — Powers, Appointment & Electoral Reforms
prelimsNote: Art 324: superintendence of elections to Parliament, State legislatures, and offices of President and Vice-President — NOT Panchayats/Municipalities (State Election Commissions, Arts 243K/243ZA).
Multi-member since 1993; CEC removable only like an SC judge, other ECs only on the CEC's recommendation.
Chief Election Commissioner and Other ECs Act 2023: selection by PM, Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet minister (Anoop Baranwal 2023 had included the CJI).
Art 329: courts cannot question delimitation laws; Delimitation Commission orders have the force of law and cannot be challenged (UPSC 2012).

nodes.title: Paid News, Model Code of Conduct & Electoral Finance
prelimsNote: Model Code of Conduct is not statutory — evolved by consensus (first in Kerala 1960), enforced by ECI from announcement of polls.
Electoral bonds scheme struck down in Feb 2024 (ADR v Union of India).
Expenditure limits apply to candidates, not to political parties.
RPA s.29C: parties must report donations above ₹20,000.

nodes.title: CAG of India — Role, Independence & Audit Functions
prelimsNote: Arts 148–151: appointed by the President; removable only like an SC judge; tenure 6 years or age 65.
Not eligible for further office under the Union or States; salary charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Audits accounts of the Union, States and bodies substantially financed by them; reports to President/Governor (Art 151) → examined by PAC.
Unlike the UK, the Indian CAG has no control over the issue of money — only an auditor (UPSC 2012 trap).

nodes.title: UPSC — Appointment, Functions & Civil Services Reforms
prelimsNote: Arts 315–323; chairman and members appointed by the President; removal by President after SC inquiry for misbehaviour (Art 317).
Tenure 6 years or age 65; chairman not eligible for further government employment (a member can become chairman of UPSC/SPSC).
Advisory body — not consulted on reservation of posts for backward classes (Art 320(4)).
Joint PSC for two or more states can be created by Parliament on the states' request (statutory).

nodes.title: Finance Commission — Constitutional Role & Recommendations
prelimsNote: Constitutional body under Art 280 — President constitutes it every 5 years; also recommends measures to augment State Consolidated Funds for local bodies (73rd/74th Amendments).
Members' qualifications fixed by Parliament (Act of 1951); recommendations not binding.
15th FC (2021–26) devolution 41%; 16th FC (Arvind Panagariya) for 2026–31 (as of 2025).
Trap: State Finance Commission (Art 243I) is a different body — reviews finances of Panchayats/Municipalities.

nodes.title: National Commission for SC/ST — Functions & Effectiveness
prelimsNote: NCSC (Art 338) and NCST (Art 338A, separated by the 89th Amendment 2003) are constitutional bodies; reports go to the President.
NCBC became constitutional (Art 338B) by the 102nd Amendment 2018 (UPSC 2023: only NCBC among NCBC/NHRC/Law Commission/NCDRC is constitutional).
They have powers of a civil court while investigating complaints.
National Commission for Women and for Minorities are statutory, not constitutional.

nodes.title: SEBI — Powers, Functions & Securities Market Regulation
prelimsNote: Set up in 1988 (non-statutory); statutory under the SEBI Act 1992.
Regulates credit rating agencies — NOT the RBI (UPSC 2022 trap).
Appeals from SEBI orders lie to the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
Regulates FPIs; Participatory Notes are issued by registered FPIs to overseas investors (UPSC 2019).

nodes.title: RBI — Autonomy, Functions & Monetary Policy (GS2)
prelimsNote: Established 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act 1934; nationalised 1949; Governor appointed by the Central Government (UPSC 2021).
The Centre's power to give directions comes from Sec 7 of the RBI Act — not from the Constitution (UPSC 2021 trap).
Monetary Policy Committee (6 members: 3 RBI, 3 government-appointed); inflation target 4% ±2% (2016 amendment).
RBI is the lender of last resort to banks in temporary crisis (UPSC 2021).

nodes.title: CBI — Appointment, Autonomy vs Accountability
prelimsNote: Set up in 1963 by a Home Ministry resolution — not a statutory body; powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946.
Director selected by a committee of the PM, Leader of Opposition (or leader of the largest opposition party) and CJI or nominee (Lokpal Act 2013).
Needs State consent to investigate in a State (Sec 6 DSPE Act); several states have withdrawn general consent.
Director's tenure: minimum 2 years, extendable up to 5 years (2021 amendment).

nodes.title: CVC — Anti-Corruption Role & Effectiveness
prelimsNote: Set up in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation; statutory under the CVC Act 2003.
Selection committee: PM, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha.
Tenure 4 years or age 65; supervises CBI in Prevention of Corruption Act cases.
Advisory; not an investigating agency itself.

nodes.title: TRAI — Telecom Regulation & Net Neutrality
prelimsNote: TRAI Act 1997; appellate functions moved to TDSAT (2000 amendment).
Net neutrality: DoT accepted TRAI's recommendations in 2018, prohibiting discriminatory treatment of content.
Telecommunications Act 2023 replaced the Indian Telegraph Act 1885.
TRAI recommends on spectrum and tariffs; licensing remains with DoT.

nodes.title: IRDA — Insurance Regulation
prelimsNote: IRDAI set up under the IRDA Act 1999 (Malhotra Committee recommendation).
Regulates insurance; pension is regulated by PFRDA (2013 Act) — a common trap.
Headquartered in Hyderabad.
Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act 2015 raised the FDI cap in insurance (later raised further).

nodes.title: National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) — Functions & Limitations
prelimsNote: Statutory — Protection of Human Rights Act 1993; chairperson a former CJI or former SC judge (2019 amendment).
Appointed by the President on a committee of PM, Speaker, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, Leaders of Opposition of both Houses and the Home Minister.
Cannot inquire into matters more than one year old; limited role over the armed forces; recommendations not binding.
Law Commission is an executive (non-statutory) body — not like NHRC (UPSC 2023).

nodes.title: Central & State Information Commissions — RTI Implementation
prelimsNote: RTI Act 2005: Central Information Commission is statutory, not constitutional.
CIC and ICs appointed by the President on a committee of PM, Leader of Opposition and a Union Minister nominated by the PM.
RTI (Amendment) Act 2019: tenure, salary and conditions now prescribed by the Central Government.
CIC (2013) held six national parties to be public authorities under RTI.

nodes.title: National Green Tribunal (NGT) — Jurisdiction & Effectiveness
prelimsNote: NGT Act 2010 — rooted in Art 21 (right to a healthy environment); principal bench at New Delhi (UPSC 2012, 2018).
Hears civil cases under seven laws (Water, Air, EP Act, Forest Conservation, Biodiversity, Water Cess, Public Liability Insurance) — NOT the Wildlife Protection Act or Forest Rights Act.
Appeal against NGT orders lies to the Supreme Court within 90 days.
Bound by principles of natural justice, not the Code of Civil Procedure; follows the polluter-pays and precautionary principles.

nodes.title: Lokpal & Lokayukta — Constitutional Status & Implementation
prelimsNote: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013: statutory, not constitutional; chairperson + up to 8 members (half judicial, half from SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women).
Selection committee: PM, Speaker, Leader of Opposition, CJI or nominee, an eminent jurist.
PM covered, with exclusions (international relations, security, public order, atomic energy, space).
First Lokpal appointed in 2019 (Justice P.C. Ghose).

nodes.title: NITI Aayog — Role, Structure vs Planning Commission
prelimsNote: Set up 1 Jan 2015 by a Union Cabinet resolution — neither constitutional nor statutory (like the Planning Commission of 1950).
Chaired by the PM; Governing Council of all CMs and LGs.
A think tank — does not allocate funds to states (unlike the Planning Commission).
Atal Innovation Mission is under NITI Aayog (UPSC 2019).

nodes.title: Zonal Councils — Purpose & Relevance
prelimsNote: Statutory — States Reorganisation Act 1956; five Zonal Councils: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern.
Chaired by the Union Home Minister; CMs of member states as vice-chairmen in rotation.
Advisory bodies for Centre–State and inter-state cooperation.
North Eastern Council is separate — statutory under the NEC Act 1971 (Sikkim included in 2002).

nodes.title: Separation of Powers — Indian Context vs USA/UK
nodes.module: Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances
prelimsNote: Not expressly stated in the Constitution, but implied; Art 50 (DPSP) separates the judiciary from the executive.
No rigid separation in India (Ram Jawaya Kapur 1955) — executive drawn from the legislature.
USA: rigid separation; UK: fusion of executive and legislature.
Separation of powers is part of the basic structure (Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain 1975).

nodes.title: Checks & Balances in Indian Constitution
nodes.module: Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances
prelimsNote: Judicial review (Art 13) checks legislature and executive; impeachment and removal procedures check the President and judges.
Art 121/211: no discussion in legislatures of the conduct of SC/HC judges except on a removal motion.
Art 122/212: courts cannot inquire into the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedural irregularity.
Financial checks: CAG audit → PAC; parliamentary questions and motions check the executive.

nodes.title: Conflict of Interest Issues in Parliament & Executive
nodes.module: Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances
prelimsNote: Office of profit: Art 102(1)(a) and Art 191(1)(a); ministers' posts are not offices of profit.
Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act 1959 lists exempted offices (UPSC 2019).
President decides an MP's disqualification on the ECI's opinion, which is binding (Art 103).
Register of Members' Interests exists in the Rajya Sabha (Ethics Committee).

nodes.title: Representation of People's Act — Key Provisions & Amendments
prelimsNote: RPA 1950: allocation of seats, delimitation, electoral rolls; RPA 1951: conduct of elections, qualifications/disqualifications, corrupt practices, disputes.
Conviction with sentence of 2+ years disqualifies from the date of conviction until 6 years after release — not permanently (Lily Thomas 2013; UPSC 2020).
A candidate can contest from at most two constituencies (s.33(7)) — UPSC 2021.
Any person registered as an elector can file a nomination; election petitions go to the High Court within 45 days.

nodes.title: Electoral Reforms — State Funding, NOTA, Compulsory Voting
prelimsNote: NOTA introduced in 2013 (PUCL v Union of India); NOTA votes do not invalidate the election.
VVPAT with EVMs mandated in a phased manner after Subramanian Swamy (2013).
Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) recommended partial state funding of elections.
Voting is not compulsory for Parliament/Assembly elections; UPSC's key (2017) treats the right to vote as a constitutional right (Art 326) — not a fundamental right or a duty.

nodes.title: Anti-Defection Law — Issues & Reform Needed
prelimsNote: Same law as node 193 — Tenth Schedule; merger exemption needs 2/3 of the legislature party.
Presiding officer's decision is subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan 1992); no statutory time limit (UPSC 2022).
Disqualified members cannot hold remunerative political posts (91st Amendment) until re-elected.
Reform debate: deciding authority should shift to ECI/President (suggested by commissions).

nodes.title: Office of Profit — Constitutional Provisions & Controversies
prelimsNote: 'Office of profit' is not defined in the Constitution; tests evolved by courts (appointment by government, remuneration, control).
Disqualification under Art 102(1)(a) / 191(1)(a) unless exempted by law (Act of 1959; UPSC 2019).
President decides on ECI opinion (Art 103); Governor decides for MLAs on ECI opinion (Art 192).
Jaya Bachchan v Union of India 2006: if an office carries remuneration, it is an office of profit even if not drawn.

nodes.title: Political Parties — Registration, Regulation & RTI
prelimsNote: Registration by ECI under s.29A RPA 1951; recognition as national/state party under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order 1968.
Political parties were first mentioned in the Constitution via the Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment 1985).
ECI cannot de-register a party except in limited cases (INC v Institute of Social Welfare 2002).
Election expenditure limits apply to candidates, not parties.

newNodesToCreate.title: Schedules of the Constitution (First to Twelfth)
prelimsNote: 1st: States & UTs; 2nd: emoluments of President, Governors, judges, CAG etc.; 3rd: forms of oaths & affirmations; 4th: allocation of Rajya Sabha seats.
5th: administration of Scheduled Areas & STs; 6th: tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram; 7th: Union, State & Concurrent Lists.
8th: 22 languages (Sindhi by 21st, Konkani/Manipuri/Nepali by 71st, Bodo/Dogri/Maithili/Santhali by 92nd Amendment); 9th: added by the 1st Amendment (1951) for land reforms.
10th: anti-defection (52nd, 1985); 11th: Panchayats — 29 subjects (73rd); 12th: Municipalities — 18 subjects (74th).
Trap: First Schedule is not about oaths (that is the Third); provisions on tribal areas of 'certain States' are in the Sixth, not Ninth (CDS 2022).

newNodesToCreate.title: Political Theory — Constitutionalism, Rule of Law, Liberty, Equality, Rights
prelimsNote: Constitutional government = limited government; chief purpose of a constitution is to define and limit the powers of government (UPSC 2020, 2021, 2023).
Rule of law (Dicey): absence of arbitrary power, equality before law, liberty of individuals protected by courts (UPSC 2018).
Equality implies absence of privileges; rights are claims of citizens against the State and are correlative with duties (UPSC 2017).
Liberty is not absence of restraint: law both limits and creates conditions for liberty (UPSC 2018, 2019).
Democracy's superior virtue: it promotes the dignity and capacity of the common people (UPSC 2017).

newNodesToCreate.title: Citizenship — Part II (Arts 5–11) & Citizenship Act 1955
prelimsNote: Single citizenship (borrowed from UK) — no separate state citizenship; Arts 5–8 dealt with citizenship at commencement.
Art 9: a person voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship ceases to be an Indian citizen; Art 11: Parliament regulates citizenship by law.
Citizenship Act 1955 — acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory; loss by renunciation, termination, deprivation.
OCI is not dual citizenship — no voting rights or constitutional offices; Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 relaxed naturalisation for six minority communities from three neighbouring countries.
Trap: only citizens can hold offices like President, Vice-President, judges, Governor, AG (UPSC 2021).

newNodesToCreate.title: Union & its Territory (Arts 1–4)
prelimsNote: Art 1: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'; territory of India = States, UTs and acquired territories.
Art 2: admission of new states (e.g. Sikkim, 36th Amendment 1975); Art 3: Parliament can reorganise States by simple majority on the President's recommendation.
State legislature's views under Art 3 are NOT binding; Art 4 — such laws are not constitutional amendments under Art 368.
Cession of Indian territory needs a constitutional amendment (Berubari 1960; 100th Amendment 2015).

newNodesToCreate.title: Local Government — Panchayati Raj (73rd Amendment)
prelimsNote: Part IX (Arts 243–243O) added by the 73rd Amendment 1992; Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects; Art 40 (DPSP) was the original basis.
Three-tier structure; the intermediate tier may be omitted in States with population under 20 lakh; Gram Sabha (Art 243A).
Reservation: SC/ST in proportion to population, at least one-third for women; minimum age 21; 5-year term, fresh election within 6 months of dissolution.
State Election Commission conducts elections (Art 243K); State Finance Commission reviews Panchayat finances and recommends sharing of taxes/grants (Art 243I); audit is by State law (Art 243J).
PESA Act 1996 extends Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with special Gram Sabha powers (UPSC 2012, 2013).

newNodesToCreate.title: Local Government — Municipalities (74th Amendment)
prelimsNote: Part IXA (Arts 243P–243ZG) added by the 74th Amendment 1992; Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects.
Three types: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area).
Ward committees for municipalities with population 3 lakh or more; District Planning Committee (Art 243ZD); Metropolitan Planning Committee for 10 lakh+ (Art 243ZE).
One-third seats reserved for women; elections by the State Election Commission (Art 243ZA).

newNodesToCreate.title: Scheduled & Tribal Areas — Fifth & Sixth Schedules, PESA
prelimsNote: Fifth Schedule (Art 244(1)): Scheduled Areas declared by Presidential Order; Governor reports annually to the President — not CMs to the Home Ministry (UPSC 2023).
Tribes Advisory Council (up to 20 members, three-fourths ST MLAs) in States with Scheduled Areas; Governor can modify central/state laws for these areas.
Sixth Schedule (Art 244(2)): Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — Autonomous District Councils (up to 30 members, 4 nominated by Governor).
Samatha 1997: transfer of tribal land to private parties in Scheduled Areas barred (UPSC 2019); PVTGs — 75 groups across 18 States + 1 UT (UPSC 2019).
Fifth Schedule status prevents transfer of tribal land to non-tribals — it does not create a UT or special-category State (UPSC 2022).

newNodesToCreate.title: Co-operative Societies (97th Amendment)
prelimsNote: 97th Amendment 2011: right to form co-operatives in Art 19(1)(c), Art 43B (DPSP), Part IXB (Arts 243ZH–243ZT).
Union of India v Rajendra Shah 2021: Part IXB struck down for State co-operatives (lacked State ratification) — survives only for multi-state co-operatives.
Board: maximum 21 directors, 5-year term; reservation for SC/ST and women on boards.
Never asked in UPSC Prelims so far — a likely gap (Ministry of Co-operation created 2021).

newNodesToCreate.title: Union Territories & Special Provisions (Arts 239–241, 370–371J)
prelimsNote: UTs administered by the President through an administrator (Art 239); Puducherry legislature under Art 239A; Delhi's special status under Art 239AA (69th Amendment 1991).
Parliament can establish a High Court for a UT or extend a State HC's jurisdiction (Art 241).
Arts 371–371J: special provisions for certain States (e.g. Maharashtra & Gujarat, Nagaland, Sikkim, Karnataka's Hyderabad-Karnataka region).
J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 created two UTs; abrogation of Art 370's special status upheld by the SC in Dec 2023.

newNodesToCreate.title: Parliament — Financial Procedure (Budget, Money & Finance Bills)
prelimsNote: The word 'Budget' is not in the Constitution — Art 112 'Annual Financial Statement'; charged expenditure (e.g. President's emoluments, judges' salaries, CAG) is not voted on.
Consolidated Fund (Art 266(1)) needs appropriation by law; Public Account (Art 266(2)) needs no appropriation; Contingency Fund (Art 267) is at the President's disposal.
Cut motions: policy cut (₹1), economy cut, token cut (₹100); vote on account (Art 116) covers only expenditure, an interim budget covers both receipts and expenditure (UPSC 2011).
Defeat of a budget/money bill in Lok Sabha means loss of confidence — the government must resign (UPSC 2012).
FRBM Act 2003 requires Medium-term Fiscal Policy and Fiscal Policy Strategy Statements with the Budget (UPSC 2020).

newNodesToCreate.title: Vice-President of India
prelimsNote: Arts 63–71; elected by an electoral college of all members of both Houses — including nominated members, but NOT State MLAs.
Ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; acts as President for up to 6 months when the office is vacant.
Removal: Rajya Sabha resolution passed by effective majority and agreed to by Lok Sabha by simple majority; 14 days' notice; no grounds specified.
Disputes about election are decided by the Supreme Court; term 5 years, eligible for re-election.

newNodesToCreate.title: Attorney General, Solicitor General & Advocate General
prelimsNote: Art 76: AG appointed by the President, qualified to be an SC judge; holds office during the President's pleasure — no fixed tenure, no constitutional rule to resign with the government (UPSC 2022).
Art 88: AG can speak and take part in proceedings of either House and committees but has no vote; enjoys parliamentary privileges (Art 105(4)) (UPSC 2013).
AG is not a member of the Cabinet and can do private practice (not against the Government of India).
Solicitor General and Additional SGs are statutory/executive law officers, not constitutional; Advocate General of a State under Art 165.
Trap: AG and SG are NOT the only non-members allowed in Parliament — ministers who are members of the other House also speak (UPSC 2022).

newNodesToCreate.title: Tribunals — Arts 323A/323B & CAT
prelimsNote: Arts 323A (administrative tribunals) and 323B (other matters) added by the 42nd Amendment 1976.
Central Administrative Tribunal set up in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act 1985 (UPSC 2011).
L. Chandra Kumar 1997: tribunal decisions are subject to High Court judicial review (Arts 226/227).
Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 abolished several appellate tribunals and standardised tenure.

newNodesToCreate.title: Other Statutory & Regulatory Bodies (FSSAI, QCI, BIS, Commodity Boards, Coal Controller)
prelimsNote: FSSAI: Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954; under the Ministry of Health (UPSC 2018).
Quality Council of India (1997): set up by the GoI jointly with ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI (UPSC 2017).
Tea Board: statutory (Tea Act 1953) under the Ministry of Commerce — not Agriculture; head office in Kolkata (UPSC 2022).
Coal Controller's Organisation: main source of coal statistics, monitors captive blocks, hears objections on coal-bearing area acquisition (UPSC 2022).
BIS mark is mandatory for automotive tyres & tubes; AGMARK is issued by the Directorate of Marketing & Inspection, not FAO (UPSC 2017).

newNodesToCreate.title: National Symbols, Flag Code & Official Language
prelimsNote: Flag Code of India 2002 (amended 2022): length-to-height ratio 3:2; machine-made and polyester flags allowed (UPSC 2023).
'Satyameva Jayate' is from the Mundaka Upanishad; National Anthem and Song adopted 24 Jan 1950.
Official Language: Part XVII (Arts 343–351) — Hindi in Devanagari; Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages.
National awards are not 'titles' under Art 18 (Balaji Raghavan 1996) (UPSC 2021).
